notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Jeremiah 26. I ran out of searches before I could check several sites. That means there's nothing here from a Pentecostal, Lutheran or Orthodox teacher. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, and nothing from bibleodyssey.org. The NET Bible page I found showed only its translation, not its scholarly notes.

**Chapter overview**
- Most commentators link this chapter to the temple sermon in chapter 7. Guzik says it seems to be the same message he preached in Jeremiah 7. In Jeremiah 26, the emphasis is on the hostile response to this sermon at the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- The Gospel Coalition's commentary agrees. It says chapter 7 is about what Jeremiah said, and chapter 26 is about how people reacted. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/
- Some disagree. Keil and Delitzsch point out that Jeremiah often repeated his main themes, so they don't think the Shiloh warning proves the two sermons are the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm
- The Restoration Commentary thinks chapter 7 is an earlier sermon from King Josiah's reign and chapter 26 a later one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-7.html
- Constable notes that verses 8–16 are the only complete trial account in the Old Testament. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-26.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Jehoiakim became king in 609 BC, about four years before Babylon first invaded. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Teachers differ on the date. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Uriah's flight and capture (vv. 20–23) took time. So "the beginning of the reign" probably means Jehoiakim's second or third year, not his first days. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase just means the earlier part of his reign, with no exact year given. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm
- Utley points out that the book isn't in time order: chapter 25 is dated to Jehoiakim's fourth year, while 26:1 is earlier. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-26

**v. 2**
- Guzik quotes John Trapp, who calls the command not to leave out a word "a mirror for ministers", meaning preachers must deliver everything God gives them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Matthew Henry says nobody should call Jeremiah careless for preaching in the temple court. God ordered it, even though the priests, his enemies, controlled that space. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Keil and Delitzsch: Jeremiah was to give God's word in full, without softening the threat. The "court" may have been the outer court where ordinary people gathered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm
- Utley: the Hebrew word means "diminish," which suggests a very specific message from God. He compares Deuteronomy 4:2. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-26
- Haydock (a Catholic commentary), citing Calmet, says every pastor facing danger should follow this example. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/jeremiah/26.htm

**v. 3 (where traditions differ: does God "relent"?)**
- Guzik: God already knew whether Judah would repent; Jeremiah didn't. God wanted him to preach in real hope that they would listen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Coffman quotes Feinberg: God's call to repent is always individual, and promises of divine judgment are always conditional. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-26.html
- **Reformed view.** These articles discuss passages where God "relents" in general, not Jeremiah 26 itself. Ligonier says God's mind never changes, because God doesn't change, has one complete plan and knows everything. It quotes Gill: God changes how he deals with people, and "repentance" is said of him only in human terms. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/does-god-change-his-mind
- R.C. Sproul says God isn't talked into changing his mind. He simply does what he always promised: he doesn't punish sinners who repent. https://www.monergism.com/does-god-change-his-mind
- **Evangelical view.** GotQuestions separates conditional warnings from fixed decrees. It cites Jeremiah 18:7–11 and says God stays fully consistent: he forgives those who repent and judges those who don't. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-change-mind.html
- **Open theism.** Don Stewart notes that people who hold the "open view" of God see stories like this as God really changing his mind. He sets this against the traditional view that God knew all along. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/27-did-god-change-his-mind-about-nineveh.cfm
- **Catholic view.** Haydock says the "if" doesn't mean God is ignorant. Citing St. Jerome, it says God keeps human free will, and the threat is conditional on people carrying on in sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/jeremiah/26.htm
- Jimmy Akin on catholic.com (writing generally) also says God doesn't truly change his mind; the Bible describes him in human terms. https://www.catholic.com/audio/caf/does-god-change-his-mind
- **Methodist view.** Wesley's Notes say nothing on this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/26.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: right after telling Jeremiah to preach as if they might listen, God has him warn what will happen if they don't hear and obey. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/

**v. 5**
- Utley links "listen to … my servants the prophets" to Deuteronomy 18:19. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-26

**v. 6**
- Matthew Poole: the tabernacle and the ark stood at Shiloh. God left it (Psalm 78:60), and now he threatens the same for the temple the people trusted in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm
- Gill and the Geneva Bible explain "a curse": other nations would curse people by saying, "May God do to you what he did to Jerusalem." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm
- The Cambridge Bible contrasts this with God's promise in Genesis 12:3 that Abraham's family would be a blessing to the nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm
- Utley makes the same point: God's people were meant to bless the world, but the nations would see only judgment. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-26
- Ellicott: the shock and anger suggest the people were hearing this for the first time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Benson: "the prophets" here are false prophets, who claimed to be prophets without being sent by God. "The house of the LORD" means the outer courts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-7.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik quotes Thompson: the Hebrew verb for "gathered" can mean gathering for war or with hostile intent, which shows how angry the crowd was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Coffman: the priests and prophets put two capital charges in the crowd's mouth. First, that Jeremiah spoke in God's name without authority. Second, that he predicted the fall of a city and temple they claimed God had promised to protect. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-26.html
- Matthew Henry: in repeating his words, they left out God's "I will" and the condition "if you will not listen." He compares this with the charges against Jesus and Stephen. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- The Gospel Coalition: they seem to have charged him with blasphemy, treating words against God's institutions as words against God (Leviticus 24:16). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/
- Haydock: their excuse sounded believable, since God seemed to have promised the temple would last forever (1 Kings 9:3). Jesus faced a similar charge (Matthew 26:61). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/jeremiah/26.htm

**v. 10**
- Wesley: the officials came from the palace when they heard about the uproar. The entrance of the gate was where the court that judged false prophets usually sat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/26.htm
- Coffman thinks the officials arriving was providential, and that without them it would have been a mock trial. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-26.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik: they saw Jeremiah as a traitor who weakened morale and helped Jerusalem's enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Wesley: when nations are corrupt, religious officials have always been the worst enemies of God's faithful ministers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/26.htm
- The Bible Hub summary links the charge to Deuteronomy 18:20, the law against prophets who speak without God's authority. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/jeremiah/26.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: Jeremiah makes clear his message wasn't his own choice; God sent him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: Jeremiah didn't water down his message or beg for mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the word the accusers used against him can also be read as "concerning." Jeremiah takes it in that better sense, which leaves room for repentance. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm

**v. 13**
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah's words were a fair warning, not a final sentence. If they listened, the judgment could be avoided. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Guzik: Jeremiah spoke as if *they* were the ones on trial, and in a real sense they were. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/

**v. 14**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this shows Jeremiah's humility and submission to the authorities (Romans 13:1). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Coffman compares this to Jesus, who submitted to the authorities while warning them of the consequences. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-26.html
- Pulpit Commentary (D. Young): Jeremiah was neither eager to live nor afraid to die. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-26.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: killing God's prophet would only add to the city's guilt. He passes on Trapp's list of five virtues in Jeremiah's defence: prudence, love, humility, courage and fearlessness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Matthew Henry: people who persecute God's ministers harm themselves more than the ministers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: they didn't like the message, but had to admit it came from God. He contrasts this with Jesus, who was condemned even after a similar warning about innocent blood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Matthew Henry asks: if they agreed he spoke for God, why didn't they change their ways? https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Haydock (citing Worthington): crowds change easily, for better or worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/jeremiah/26.htm

**vv. 17–18**
- Wesley: this is the Micah whose book is in the Bible. The words quoted are from Micah 3:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/26.htm
- Guzik: Micah also warned against false prophets who said no harm could come to Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Haydock: the elders were recalling events about 100 years earlier. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/jeremiah/26.htm
- Utley gives an alternative translation of the last phrase ("a mere wooded ridge") and suggests it may hint at the sacred groves of fertility worship. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-26

**v. 19**
- Guzik: Hezekiah feared God, and God relented. The elders saw it was in their own interest not to persecute Jeremiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Wesley: "great evil against our souls" means harm to ourselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/26.htm
- Matthew Henry: it is good to hold ourselves back from sin by thinking of the damage it does to our own souls. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm

**v. 20 (who tells Uriah's story? Teachers disagree)**
- Calvin lists several readings. Hostile people may have raised Uriah's death to push for Jeremiah's. Or the elders may have used it to show that killing God's prophet only adds crime to crime. Calvin himself leans toward the second. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/26-20.html
- Wesley thinks these are probably the words of Jeremiah's enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/jeremiah/26.htm
- Gill: the people swung against Jeremiah again after hearing Uriah's case, and only Ahikam's influence stopped them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/26-24.html
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees with both. It says verses 20–23 only look like part of the elders' speech. They can't fit "the beginning of the reign," and they belong with v. 24 as the writer's own comment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-20.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown mention this "writer's comment" view (from Glassius) but think the context fits a continuation of the elders' speech. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Kiriath-jearim was a town in Judah on the western border of Benjamin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/26-20.htm

**v. 21**
- Matthew Henry: by fleeing, Uriah showed distrust of God and the fear of man that "brings a snare." Fleeing to Egypt was especially unfitting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Benson (in Spanish on this page) also blames weak faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/26-20.html
- The Pulpit Commentary homilies (same page, also in Spanish): sometimes it is safer to face danger than run. Jeremiah stood firm and lived; Uriah fled and was killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/26-20.html
- Constable: this shows that Israel's leaders opposed all true prophets, and how much danger Jeremiah was in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-26.html

**v. 22**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Pharaoh had put Jehoiakim on the throne (2 Kings 23:34), which explains why Egypt handed Uriah over. Uriah was faithful in his message but wrong to leave his post. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Guzik's Jeremiah 36 notes quote a suggestion that Elnathan later felt remorse for his part. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-36/

**v. 23**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: prophets seem to have had their own burial place (Matthew 23:29). Uriah was denied it so people wouldn't regard him as a true prophet. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Calvin: the "graves of the common people" were a place of dishonour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-26.html

**v. 24**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Ahikam was one of the men King Josiah sent to ask God about the newly found book of the law (2 Kings 22:12). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Barnes: Ahikam's son Gemariah lent Jeremiah a room for reading the scroll, and his son Gedaliah later became governor. Clarke suggests Ahikam may have had to hide Jeremiah from the crowd. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/26-24.html
- Calvin: "hand" means effort. Ahikam saved Jeremiah only with great and hard struggle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-26.html
- Guzik: Ahikam was perhaps one of the elders. Jeremiah needed protection from the mob as well as the court. Jesus had no Ahikam to defend Him. Jesus is our Ahikam, defending us from every accusation of the evil one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-26/
- Matthew Henry: God can raise up powerful people to protect good people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_026.cfm
- Constable: the same priests later put Jesus and the apostles on trial for speaking about the temple's destruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-26.html
